question: In which layer of the uterus does uterine cancer most commonly start?
explanation: Spot on! The endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus, and that is where most uterine cancers begin. Keep up the great work!

question: Why is uterine cancer often caught early when it is easier to treat?

options.A: It causes noticeable symptoms early in its development.
options.B: It grows extremely slowly compared to other cancers.
options.C: Pain occurs before any abnormal bleeding starts.
options.D: Routine blood tests screen for it every year.

explanation: You got it! Abnormal bleeding usually shows up early, which alerts patients and doctors to check things out quickly.

question: What is the most common type of uterine cancer?
explanation: Brilliant! Endometrial adenocarcinoma makes up the vast majority of all diagnosed uterine cancers.

question: What is the main difference between Type I and Type II endometrial cancers?

options.A: Type I is estrogen-dependent and low-grade, while Type II is aggressive and estrogen-independent.
options.B: Type I affects the muscle layer, while Type II affects the outer covering.
options.C: Type II responds very well to hormone therapy, while Type I does not respond at all.
options.D: Type I occurs only in younger women, while Type II occurs exclusively during pregnancy.

explanation: Well done! Type I is fueled by estrogen and grows slowly, while Type II is tougher, faster-growing, and doesn't rely on estrogen.

question: Which hormone imbalance is a main trigger for most endometrial cancers?

options.C: High levels of progesterone with low estrogen

explanation: Spot on! When estrogen has no progesterone to balance it out, the uterine lining thickens too much, raising cancer risk.

question: Which patient has the highest risk of developing endometrial cancer?

options.A: A 22-year-old athlete using combination oral contraceptives
options.B: A 65-year-old obese woman with a history of late menopause
options.C: A 30-year-old woman who has given birth to four children
options.D: A 45-year-old woman with regular 28-day menstrual cycles

explanation: Correct! Older age, obesity, and late menopause all mean a longer time of being exposed to estrogen without a break.

question: What is the most common early sign of endometrial cancer?
explanation: You nailed it! Any bleeding or spotting after menopause is a red flag that always needs a doctor's attention.

question: As a nurse, why should you immediately report even minor spotting in a postmenopausal woman?

options.A: It proves the patient has a severe clotting disorder.
options.B: It is a classic warning sign of endometrial malignancy.
options.C: It means the patient has stopped taking estrogen replacement.
options.D: It always indicates an advanced, incurable tumor stage.

explanation: Great job! Spotting after menopause is never normal and acts as the main clue that triggers testing for uterine cancer.

question: Which procedure gives the final, sure diagnosis for uterine cancer?
explanation: Spot on! Taking a small tissue sample through a biopsy lets the lab confirm if cancer cells are present.

question: Why do doctors often order a transvaginal ultrasound when a patient has abnormal bleeding?

options.A: To measure the thickness of the endometrial lining
options.B: To measure circulating hormone levels in the blood
options.C: To remove small tumors without surgery
options.D: To check for metastasis in the lungs and liver

explanation: Correct! A thick uterine lining seen on ultrasound helps doctors decide if a tissue biopsy is needed next.

question: What is the primary surgical treatment for uterine cancer?

options.B: Partial resection of the uterine cervix only
options.C: Removal of both ovaries while leaving the uterus intact
options.D: Cryotherapy and laser ablation of the endometrium

explanation: You got it! Standard surgery means taking out the uterus, Fallopian tubes, and ovaries to treat the cancer safely.

question: When would a patient with uterine cancer likely need radiation or chemotherapy after surgery?

options.A: As a replacement for surgery when the patient is very young
options.B: To restore normal menstrual function after the operation
options.C: If the tumor has high-risk features or has spread beyond the uterus
options.D: To prevent the initial development of benign uterine fibroids

explanation: Brilliant! Extra treatments like radiation or chemo are added if the cancer cells have started spreading further or look aggressive.

question: Which complication should a nurse watch for most closely right after a hysterectomy?
explanation: Spot on! Right after surgery, watching out for heavy bleeding (hemorrhage) and signs of infection is top priority.

question: What is the most important discharge instruction for a patient recovering from an abdominal hysterectomy?

options.A: Stop taking all prescribed pain medications immediately
options.B: Resume high-impact aerobic exercise by tomorrow
options.C: Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for several weeks
options.D: Apply heat packs to the abdomen continuously every day

explanation: You nailed it! Resting and avoiding heavy loads protects the stitches and helps the belly heal properly inside.
